2. Reported distributions after judgment

D chains and seams

D stageMembers seenJudgment
pc-arrivalL05 base → L06 deltaValid hold. Counter, windows, computer and “1983” stay fixed; crate/unpacked arrival is the story change.
retail-shelfL07 base → L08 delta → L09 deltaValid hold. The shopper mass is added beyond rails, then the shelf stock depletes. Each delta visibly advances state.
drive-memoryL13 base → L14 deltaValid hold. The closed drive opens to categorized contents.
drive-sellerL18 base → L19 delta → L20 deltaValid hold. Cashbox addition and pick-holder comparison are discrete story states on the same counter.

The fresh seam review found two missed holds: L16→L17 keeps the same pair and retail world but needlessly changes camera/set for the rivalry expression, and L24→L25 keeps the same warehouse/carton subject but needlessly changes camera/set for the close-and-label state. No authored D chain reads as a forced hold or a visual no-op: every listed delta changes a story-bearing state. Other hard cuts are supported by a change in setting, primary subject or register; the clearest examples are L11→L12 (hero drive to relational computer cutaway), L17→L18 (rival computers to supplier), and L23→L24 (reaction figure to brick reveal).

For context only, the LIKED records visibly organize L01–L04, L05–L08, L12–L15, L17–L18 and L21–L22 as holds. Those structures are comparator evidence, not rulings against D.

Every D stage record supplies a field basis, and the pixels show the named source or material. I found no dominant-axis recurrence across distinct stages that lacked a physical or story cause. This does not make every field equally attractive: L11’s green cast is especially forceful, and L18–L21 form a long ochre run, but those are viewer-feel observations rather than criterion failures.

D’s zero-figure concentration follows thing, quantity, place and absence subjects in the records. That is descriptive, not inherently preferable. The occupancy exceptions are causal rather than distributional: L09 retains a mass after the sentence’s causal subject returns to shelf depletion; L23 adds a reaction figure to a title/carton beat; L25 omits participants from an exchange/action clause.

Crowd-bounding outcomes from pixels

- D L08 and L09 both place the shopper mass beyond brass rails, at middle/rear scale, with the near queue lane empty. Both satisfy the positive geometry criterion. L09 still has the separate occupancy failure noted above because its sentence is about product depletion.

- LIKED L07 visibly keeps its mass behind the shop window with the near shop area figure-free. LIKED L08 retains that rear mass but adds a large buyer in the near zone; the transaction becomes clearer while the mass is no longer wholly receded. LIKED L10 runs a queue through the near pavement rather than beyond a bounding element. LIKED L20 spreads prospectors from foreground through background and places the merchant at the near stall, so the mass is not bounded and receded.

- LIKED records mark additional rows as crowd beats, but the pixels of L17–L18 show a pair, and L19, L21 and L22 show a single clear figure. Under the observed-figures rule, those are not treated as visible masses for a crowd-geometry outcome.

4. Register and taste axes

Frame citations use D:Lxx and LIKED:Lxx to identify the opened PNG in the two evidence sets.

Viewer-felt axisVariant DLIKED runComparative observation
Render register: paper grain, dust-beam light, painterly shading, moody grade vs flat-celCrisp contour lines, broad clean fills and relatively even illumination dominate. Texture exists in wood, kraft and brick, but atmospheric grain and falloff are restrained (D:L05, D:L07, D:L15, D:L25). The clearest mood turns are green-window workshop (D:L11) and cool warehouse (D:L23).The same illustrated family carries more dust specks, narrow beams, soft shadow falloff and graded darkness: the shop beam (LIKED:L05–L08), dusty shelf shaft (LIKED:L09), velvet spotlight (LIKED:L11), cash-yard side light (LIKED:L19) and dusk shutter (LIKED:L25).D feels closer to bright flat-cel production art; LIKED more often feels lit, dusty and materially shaded. This difference is strongest on taste-reference L05, L06, L09, L11, L19, L23 and L25.
Open air / depthD creates long constructed recession in the empty retail floor (D:L07), rival aisles (D:L16–L17), carton procession (D:L22) and cool warehouse (D:L23). Several other rows compress the world behind a large object (D:L01, D:L05, D:L11, D:L21, D:L25).LIKED repeatedly uses foreground/mid-ground/background separation: shop-to-street depth (LIKED:L05–L08), night high street (LIKED:L10), full creek camp (LIKED:L20), pallet canyon (LIKED:L21–L22) and yard/shutter air (LIKED:L25). It also permits concentrated object stages such as LIKED:L11 and LIKED:L23.D can build deeper architecture, but LIKED varies open vista and intimate hero space more often. D’s deepest views are usually clean one-point aisles; LIKED depth is more often populated by story activity or atmosphere.
Warmth and saturationD is frequently high-key cream, oak and brass (D:L05–L10, D:L15–L17), then strongly ochre (D:L18–L22). The desert yellow in D:L21 is especially saturated; D:L11 turns strongly green.LIKED’s early shop/den run is warmer and more amber (LIKED:L01–L08), while later frames use larger cool fields against selective warm sources (LIKED:L10, LIKED:L11, LIKED:L21–L23, LIKED:L25). LIKED:L20 keeps warm ochre but with shaded earth variation.D often raises overall brightness and keeps colours locally clean. LIKED uses warmer early nostalgia and stronger warm/cool contrast later, producing a moodier grade even when base saturation is modest.
Composition scaleD alternates oversized object close views (D:L01, D:L11, D:L21, D:L25) with small figures inside large retail sets (D:L16–L17). Its staged chains deliberately preserve one camera scale (D:L05–L06, D:L07–L09, D:L18–L20).LIKED shifts scale more aggressively: character close hero (LIKED:L01–L04), broad shop (LIKED:L05–L08), tight symbolic shelf (LIKED:L09), object spotlight (LIKED:L11), landscape crowd (LIKED:L20), industrial canyon (LIKED:L21–L22), reveal close-up (LIKED:L23), map (LIKED:L24) and exterior (LIKED:L25).D gains state continuity and world consistency inside stages. LIKED gains shot-to-shot scale modulation and a broader mix of visual registers.
Accent popsD uses clay red as a recurring object/material cue (D:L01, D:L03, D:L22, D:L24) and isolated clothing colour in the bounded crowd (D:L08–L09); the black “HARD DRIVE” lettering becomes the loudest mark in D:L25.LIKED uses black wig mass (LIKED:L02–L04), cyan/magenta arcade light (LIKED:L03–L04), red wax (LIKED:L15), phone glow against blue night (LIKED:L10), green cash (LIKED:L19), red brick against cool grey (LIKED:L23, LIKED:L25) and pale blue water against ochre land (LIKED:L24).LIKED’s accents more often sit against a dark or quiet field and therefore pop harder. D’s red/clay recurrence is coherent, but its brighter fields reduce contrast.
Symbolic vs literal depictionD most often physicalizes the sentence directly: hardware connection (D:L12), repeated dependency (D:L15), cashbox (D:L19), pick-holder (D:L20), drive in gold pan (D:L21), carton quantity (D:L22), brick in box (D:L24) and labelled carton (D:L25).LIKED more often transforms the idea: winged computers (LIKED:L09), drive-as-strongroom (LIKED:L12–L15), literal cash rake (LIKED:L19), full supply/prospector relationship (LIKED:L20), global route map (LIKED:L24) and brick-as-doorstop coda (LIKED:L25).D’s literal/mechanistic choices often improve immediate causal legibility, especially D:L12, D:L15 and D:L22. LIKED’s symbolic choices often add wit, scale change and after-image, especially on taste-reference L09, L19, L20, L24 and L25.

Across the 13 taste-reference rows, LIKED’s recurring signature is not a preferred figure count. It is the conjunction of selective light, warm/cool grade, visible material texture, variable scale, stronger accent isolation and symbolic staging. D sometimes retains one part of that conjunction—deep architecture in L22, red clay in L24, a small cast in L16–L17—but rarely assembles the full register in one taste-reference frame.

5. Weaknesses, attribution, and human decision

Weakest D frames first

OrderD frameWhy it is weak from pixels and record
1L10The carton on a tilted ramp in an empty bright room does not resolve to “Apple released the iPhone”; neither a release event, phone, audience nor queue is visible. The frame is clean but causally opaque.
2L25Exact lettering is successful, but the giant sealed box drops the brick reveal and does not depict selling. It also misses the obvious L24 hold, so literalness, occupancy and seam logic fail together.
3L03The compromised carton shows an actual hard-drive mechanism and a dangling red rectangular block; the red element reads as a tag or handle more readily than a brick, so the corporate-fraud foreshadow is visually muddled.
4L02The row is legible as “wigs plus arcade,” but the faceless wigs float in a ceiling cluster, making the mall feel like an icon board rather than a physically inhabited period scene.
5L23pc-boxy is clear and expressive, yet the sentence’s causal evidence—the title/carton reveal—is absent. The character consumes the near scale while the cracked box remains merely suspicious.
6L20The held counter is coherent, but a double-ended pick-shaped drive holder reads as decorative hardware rather than people selling picks and shovels. The comparison has little action or relational staging.
7L09Shelf depletion is excellent and the crowd geometry remains disciplined, but the people are no longer needed to reveal the sentence’s causal subject. The chain hold and occupancy criterion pull in different directions here.
8L11The drive identity is correct, but the green cast, cables and ring of tools diffuse the hero-object focus that the line invites.

What D improves and worsens versus LIKED

AreaD improvesD worsens
Causal legibilityClear component relation (D:L12), repeated need (D:L15), bounded demand/depletion sequence (D:L07–L09) and carton quantity (D:L22).Metaphor or action is under-shown in D:L10, D:L20, D:L23 and D:L25.
Stage continuityValid, visibly economical holds in L05–L06, L07–L09, L13–L14 and L18–L20.Missed holds at L16→L17 and L24→L25; some valid holds also lock a less evocative composition for several beats, especially L18–L20.
Occupancy and crowdThing/quantity beats are often cleanly person-free; the L16–L17 pair is scaled inside a world; L08–L09 visibly bound and recede a mass.L09 retains non-causal people, L23 inserts a non-causal reaction figure, and L25 omits transaction participants. Blurred background people in L18–L20 make the observed occupancy less clean than the record’s single-maker emphasis.
Physical palette basisEvery stage has a visible light/material cause, and turns such as L11, L13 and L23 are easy to identify.Bright even fields and repeated cream/ochre reduce mood range; physically justified colour does not by itself produce the dust, falloff or contrast of LIKED.
Viewer registerCrisp object identity, clean environments and strong one-point depth in L07, L16–L17, L22–L23.Less paper grain, less dust-beam atmosphere, flatter shading, weaker accent isolation and less scale modulation across the slice.

Attribution: criterion set versus subject/composition choice

Looks attributable to the criterion setLooks attributable mainly to subject/composition choicesMixed cases
The explicit D stages and single-state deltas; rear-zone rail geometry at L08–L09; the zero/pair/mass decisions in records; physical field+basis language visible in the lighting and materials.Flat-cel illumination, amount of grain, dust or painterly shading; choosing a ramp for L10, a pick-holder for L20, a gold pan close-up for L21, a literal brick pallet for L24 or a giant label box for L25; camera scale and accent isolation. None of those choices is required by the four criteria.L16–L17’s small pair in a large store follows occupancy/world staging, but the separate cameras create a missed hold. L18–L20’s held counter follows chain discipline, while the quiet cashbox and decorative pick are subject choices. L09’s retained crowd follows the hold while conflicting with per-sentence occupancy. Palette bases influence colour families, but the bright flat rendering of those colours remains a register choice.

Neutral human-decision menu

- Keep D’s chain, occupancy, palette-basis and crowd-geometry logic as the causal skeleton, while testing the LIKED register—dust, graded falloff, warmer/cooler contrast, material texture and quieter accent fields—without changing the acting subject.

- Keep D as the literal/mechanistic direction and treat the LIKED symbolic rows as optional alternates where wit or after-image matters more than direct explanation.

- Keep the LIKED register and symbolic vocabulary, while importing only D’s verified seam, causal-occupancy and rear-zone crowd decisions.

- Use row-selective retention: D where causal mechanism and bounded geometry are the visible strength; LIKED where atmosphere, scale modulation or symbolic compression is the visible strength.

- Hold both sets as observational evidence and request a human eye-gate on the specific tradeoff between D’s causal economy and LIKED’s atmosphere/symbolism, without converting either distribution into a target.

No option is selected here, and no overall winner is declared.
